en: In the third fascicle of Master Ji’s treatise,
within the explanation of the ten topical meanings of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), the first five have already been explained by combining the preceding two sections.
End of the section on the gates. Third, the analysis of the sixth meaning—the gate of association with mental factors (*caitta*). This contains five parts:
first, posing the question to initiate the discussion;
second, presenting the verse as the formal response.
Third, the explanation of the word "constant" (*nitya*) reveals the sequential positions where the five associations reside.
Fourth, the individual explanation of the essential nature and function of the five.
Fifth, the explanation of the meaning of "association" (*yoga*) within the verse. Alternatively, these may be divided into two parts.
First, the question;
second, the answer. Within the answer, there are two parts:
first, the presentation of the verse.
The subsequent detailed explanation. Within this detailed explanation, there are three parts:
first, the explanation of the character "constant" (*nitya*) and its five associated stages;
second, the individual analysis of the five objects.
Third, the meaning of association with mental factors.
Treatise:
With how many mental factors (caitta) is this consciousness associated?
The commentary states:
This is the first question.
[From] the Treatise:
"It is always associated with contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*).
The commentary states:
This is the response given in verse.
This refers to the phrase "corresponding to the second clause," which also applies to the five types of sensation (*pañca-vedanā*).
The following is the explanation according to the School of Exegesis (*Vyākhyā-kāra*).
Treatise:
The ālayavijñāna extends to its association with mental factors (*caitta*).
Commentary says:
This commentary explains the sequence corresponding to the root verse;
it is the third section, which interprets the character "constant" (常).
That is to say, among the three states of this fundamental consciousness (本識):
By citing the initial narrow name to explain the broad substance of consciousness,
it refers to all stages from beginningless time until the transformation [of the basis],
excluding only the state of Buddhahood.
This explains that its own substance (svabhāva) throughout its three stages is common to both [types of mind],
and it is always associated with these five mental factors (caitta).
Treatise:
Because they are subsumed under the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-citta-saṃprayukta*).
The commentary states:
Since the essence of these five is subsumed under the universal mental factors, they are necessarily associated (*saṃprayukta*).
Furthermore, although it neither increases nor decreases, it is definitively co-arisen and co-ceasing;
because it is designated as "pervasive" (sarvatraga), and because it exists during the stage of the cause, it is also not associated with other dharmas.
This shall be explained in its proper place within the following treatise.
Although the *ālayavijñāna* can be severed by those of the two vehicles,
even after it has been severed, it remains associated with only five [mental factors].
Therefore, at the stage of transformation, it is accompanied by all mental factors. The treatise states:
"Contact (sparśa) refers to the coming together of the three; its function is to serve as the basis [for feeling]."
The commentary states:
From here below is the fourth section, the detailed explanation of the five objects.
Within this, there are two parts.
First, the individual analysis of the five [aggregates] regarding their essential nature and activity;
next, the general explanation of how this acquisition (prāpti) coexists with consciousness. The individual analysis consists of two parts each;
first is the general [explanation].
Next, regarding the distinction between the individual and the general: within the general [classification], there are two different types, namely essence (*svabhāva*) and function (*karman*).
Texts such as the *Xianyang lun* (Śrāmaṇyaphala-sūtra-śāstra) are all consistent with this;
that is, they clarify the essence and manifest the function.
Treatise:
It is called the "conjunction of the three" because the faculty, the object, and consciousness meet.
Commentary: [As stated above].
Next, there are two parts to the detailed explanation below.
First, it extensively elaborates on the preceding section by refuting others. The actual essence of the "threefold conjunction" consists of the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness.
The nature [of these factors] differs, and thus they are designated as three. When they do not contradict one another but rather interact, it is called "conformity" (*anuloma*).
For example, when consciousness does not arise from its roots, or when objects arise, this is termed "contradiction" (*pratiloma*).
Furthermore, just as the three factors— the ear faculty, the visual consciousness, and the olfactory object— are not called the "conjunction of the three" when they are discordant,
if they are mutually concordant,
the three necessarily arise together.
Because they are not mutually contradictory, they are called "concordant.
The faculties can serve as a basis,
and the objects can serve as what is grasped.
Consciousness arises from two [factors]:
it depends upon the sense faculty and apprehends the object.
This interaction is termed the essence of the "threefold conjunction."
The commentary explains that contact is also called the "conjunction of the three" for two reasons.
It states: "Contact arises depending on them; therefore, it is said to be 'of them'."
The commentary states:

It is precisely by virtue of these two meanings that contact is called the "conjunction of the three. First, it arises in dependence upon them; "them" refers to the sense faculties and so forth, which are the causes of contact.
Because it depends upon the threefold conjunction, it is also called the "threefold conjunction.
Therefore, the Noble Teaching states that contact arises from the threefold conjunction.
The Abhidharma also says: "Depending on the threefold conjunction, two things cause them to conjoin; these are the sense faculties and so forth."
This is the fruit of contact (*sparśa*).

That is to say, contact enables the three factors—the sense faculty (*indriya*) and so forth—to function together as the basis (*āśraya*), the appropriation (*upādāna*), and the object of cognition (*vijñeya*) for discernment (*vijñapti*).
It is through contact that this triad is brought into conjunction.
Therefore, it is said that contact (*sparśa*) can bring together the three factors.
Based on these two meanings, contact is termed "the conjunction of the three.
It is not that a single entity of contact itself can be called "three."
Based on the cause that is contact and the result that is the conjunction [of the three], contact is said to be the coming together of those three.
Question: The object resides in the future, the sense faculty abides in the past, and consciousness dwells in the present.

Question: How is contact (sparśa) a "conjunction" (saṃnipāta)? Answer: It is called a conjunction because it acts as the basis for mutual conformity, as the act of grasping, and as that which is produced by the two [the sense organ and the object].
Does this mean that the three must actually come together and abide in one place to be called a conjunction? Or is it called a conjunction based on the predominance of the sense faculty?
There is no logical error in naming the contact that is not an equal-and-immediate [condition] as "the conjunction of the three," for the triad of faculty,
object, and consciousness is always present in the present moment.
No faculty or object exists in another time, because the two periods of the past and the future do not substantially exist. Question:
The object is in the future, while the contact is in the present.
How can it be said that contact is the fruit of those [dharmas]? Answer: Who says that what is produced is itself the fruit?
When future dharmas are being grasped in the present, they merely serve as objects conducive to the arising of the mind and so forth.

Therefore, although the manifest consciousness is designated as "arising from the object" (*ālambana*) through contact, it is not necessarily the case that what arises must be its direct fruit. Furthermore, the substance of that object exists only in the present;
thus, even though it is produced by contact with the past or future, it appears [as if it were present].
It is also called "fruit.
The preceding section explained the general contact as the conjunction of the three; hereafter, the treatise explains the aforementioned "discriminative transformation.
Treatise:
"The state of the threefold conjunction is designated as 'transformation' (*vipariṇāma*).
Commentary: This first explains transformation.
The subsequent explanation of the analysis refers to the state of the conjunction of the three—sense faculty, object, and consciousness.
It is called the "state of conjunction" because it excludes the time when they have not yet conjoined. Upon these three...
The functional activity that possesses the capacity to give rise to all mental factors (caitta) in accordance [with their conditions] is called "transformation" (anyathātva).
This refers to these three dharmas while they abide in the state of seeds and prior to their conjunction.
In all cases, there is no activity of mental factors that arise in accordance [with their conditions];
rather, their functional capacity arises only when the three [factors] conjoin.
Since this has already been explained previously...
The Jewel is said to be transformation (*pariṇāma*).
Transformation is precisely the activity within the three natures.
To correctly understand the essence of transformation is to understand that it consists of these three dharmas.
Next, the commentary explains "discrimination":
contact arises resembling that [object], and is therefore called discrimination.
The commentary states:
The function of discrimination is the activity of contact (*sparśa*);
that is to say, it resides upon contact.

The functional capacity for transformation that resembles the three preceding types of *citta* conducive to rebirth is called "discrimination" (*vikalpa*). Discrimination is precisely the apprehension of what appears to be something else;
it is like calling a son who resembles his father "the discrimination of the father. This [passage] generally indicates the three factors: the sense faculties and so forth.
The capacity to function in accordance with the mental factors (caitta) is called "transformation" (vipariṇāma).
This contact (sparśa) likewise possesses the functional activity to give rise to mental factors in accordance with them, and it experiences [the object] as resembling those three.
Therefore, this is called "discriminative transformation. Question: Above the conjunction of the three, there is a capacity that conduces to the arising of contact, which is called "transformation.
Since contact resembles that [conjunction] and possesses such a capacity, [it too is a transformation].
Furthermore, if that which arises spontaneously is called "discrimination" (*vikalpa*), what fault would there be? If that which arises spontaneously is called discrimination,
then one should state that contact (*sparśa*) takes contact as its condition,
just as there is a functional capacity for feelings (*vedanā*) to arise spontaneously.
Because it is said that the function of contact is called "discrimination" (vikalpa).
If that which is not in accord with itself is named "discrimination," why is it said to give rise to sensations and so forth?

Is it not the case that [contact] arises as something resembling [its cause]? Answer: Contact does not arise as something resembling its own cause, because the functional capacity of contact does not arise from itself;
it is like the dharmas such as sensation (vedanā), which cannot produce anything else [of their own kind].
It would then be like that which lacks a perceiver;
by analogy, the same should apply to tactile sensation.
Furthermore, because it possesses spatial limits.
That is to say, the faculties and their objects have two kinds of functional capacities: they can produce consciousness, and they can also produce other [factors].
Consciousness merely arises [from conditions] and lacks the function of self-arising;
contact should be understood in the same way.
Contact does not resemble that [consciousness] in its production of consciousness, nor does it possess the two types of functional capacity [of consciousness].
Because there is no spatial extension (pradeśa),
if one considers the arising of the aspects from the seeing and self-verifying portions,
there is likewise a semblance of an object.
Furthermore, it is like experiencing touch while not experiencing mental attention (*manasikāra*). Question:

If that which resembles the three functions is called "conceptual transformation" (*vikalpa-pariṇāma*), why is it stated in the first chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and elsewhere [that it is not]?
It is said that its essence consists in the discrimination of the transformation of the faculties.
To answer this question, the treatise next states: "It is said...
[The Treatise].
"The power of the transformation of the faculties reaches the transformation of the faculties.
Commentary: This reconciles the preceding contradiction.
This refers to the moment when contact arises, induced by the state of the threefold conjunction;
at that time, the power of the transformation of the sense faculty (*indriya*) is superior to that of the other two.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other treatises [state this].

This speaks only of the differentiation of the transformation of the faculties (*indriya*), and does not speak of the differentiation of the transformation of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and its objects (*viṣaya*). The word "etc.
(*ādi*) here includes the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. Furthermore, regarding the sixth case ending used for the faculty: it indicates that the faculty is the basis (*āśraya*) for the transformation.
This demonstrates that transformation is the function of the essence of the faculties (*indriya*).
Although the *Abhidharma* treatises distinguish the faculties based on the predominance of their functions,
they still do not fully distinguish all the capacities of the faculties.
It can only apprehend the functional capacities that correspond to the three types of feeling to be experienced in the future,
because feeling is produced immediately following contact.
As stated in the first fascicle of the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*:

Contact (*sparśa*) is able to differentiate the three—faculty, object, and consciousness—because they are conducive to the three types of feeling; thus it differentiates the arising of the three feelings, which is consistent with the text of the *Abhidharma*.
However, its differentiation of faculty, object, and consciousness is somewhat broader than that of the *Abhidharma*.
Because all possess the characteristics of the three types of feelings that arise in accordance with their conditions.

Among these, taking them collectively as being capable of resembling all [feelings] is the most thorough explanation of the principle. Furthermore, regarding what that treatise calls "discrimination" (vikalpa):
This is the meaning of "discrimination.
The faculties and so forth have the capacity to produce the states of the three types of sensation;
contact is able to discriminate and cause these three states to arise.
It is called "discrimination" (*vikalpa*) because it distinguishes between three stages;
this interpretation is excellent. Question: Why is it that among the threefold conjunction, only the sense organ (*indriya*) is preeminent? Answer: First, because it is the primary factor.
The pearl possesses a superior capacity, which is designated as its "predominance.
Second, by virtue of proximity,
it is able to closely give rise to the mind and mental factors.
Third, by way of pervasiveness:
it not only produces mental factors,
but can also produce the mind itself.
Fourth, by way of continuity:
it exists as a constant succession,
whereas the object and consciousness do not.
Therefore, although the objective realm can produce both the mind and mental factors,
because it is not primary and because it is not proximate,
[it does not serve as their direct support].
If either of these two meanings is deficient, it cannot be called "superior.
Although the mind is primary and arises in close proximity to mental factors (*caitta*),
it cannot give rise to [other] minds.
Because it does not arise from itself, it is not pervasive (*vyāpin*);
because it lacks the quality of pervasiveness, it is not supreme (*parama*).
Furthermore, both the object and consciousness do not continue in succession.
Since consciousness arises in dependence upon an object, both lack the sense of continuity;
thus they do not receive the superior name [of "organ"],
for only the faculty alone is preeminent.
Question: The function of contact (*sparśa*) can be understood as previously explained.
Yet, why cannot it share the same object of cognition (*ālambana*) as the mind?
Is it only this specific portion that is designated as "contact"?
Treatise:
The conjunction of all [factors] up to this point is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of contact (*sparśa*).
Commentary: [As stated above.]
Furthermore, there is another capacity that does not merely contact those [objects];
namely, contact (*sparśa*) is also able to bring about the conjunction of all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
The intrinsic nature of contact (*sparśa*) is that which prevents [the mental factors] from being dispersed or acting individually,
causing them to converge upon a single object.
If there were no contact (sparśa),
the mind and mental factors would each be dispersed and unable to share a common object;
that they do not disperse at present is entirely due to the efficacy of contact.
Having explained intrinsic nature,
how is the activity of contact?
Although the previously explained functional capacity is itself the activity, [it is described as such here].
Because it reveals the essence through its manifestation, it is not a door of karma.
The treatise states:
"Since it seems to accord with the arising [of cognition], its function is to serve as the basis."
The commentary states:
This very category of contact,
being similar to the threefold combination (trisaṃnipāta), possesses the functional capacity to facilitate the arising of mental factors (caitta).
It is thus able to give rise to other mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
Therefore, its function is to serve as the basis for sensation (*vedanā*) and the other [mental factors].
All such mental factors as sensation depend upon this [contact] for their arising.
If non-arising were not capable of being the basis [of cognition],
how is this known? The treatise states:
The *Udayavyaya-sūtra* states that [feeling] has contact as its condition.
The commentary says:
The sūtra that elucidates arising and ceasing is called the *Udayavyaya-sūtra*.
The title of the sutra is established based on what is clarified therein.
If contact were capable of producing only feeling and nothing else,
then the other two aggregates would not have contact as their basis.
Since there are no mental factors (*caitta*) at the moment when mindless states arise, all mental factors take contact (*sparśa*) as their basis.
Therefore, the treatise says that they arise upon reaching a state of conjunction.
The commentary states:

Based on the preceding reasoning and scripture, the sūtras further teach that consciousness, contact, sensation, and so forth arise from the conjunction of two, three, or four factors. As stated in the sūtras: "With the eye and visible forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises."
It is taught that consciousness arises from the conjunction of two factors: the sense faculty and the object.
Although the Sūtra further states that consciousness arises by the power of attention (*manasikāra*), this is not mentioned here because it serves to clarify the basis [of consciousness].
That [mental factor] is able to alert the mind and exists in dependence upon the mind;
because it does not depend on the mind as its basis, it is not mentioned here. Question: Contact arises from the conjunction of the three, and is termed "discriminative transformation."

The consciousness that arises based on the conjunction of these two is called the "discerning faculty" (*vijñānendriya*). Answer: This may also be the case according to the principle of contact (*sparśa*);
however, because it is the primary factor, it differs from contact.
Both interpretations are valid.
Furthermore, the sūtra states that contact arises from the "conjunction of the three";
it explains that contact is produced by the coming together of the three factors: the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness.
The *Udayavyaya Sūtra* states that feeling (*vedanā*) and the other [mental factors] all have contact (*sparśa*) as their condition;

this means that feeling and the others arise from the conjunction of four factors: the sense faculty, the object, consciousness, and contact. Question: If there is no self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*), [how can these be established]?
It may be said that the mind arises from the conjunction of two [factors].
Since self-cognition exists,
the mind also depends upon the mind.
The essence of the mind is likewise produced from the conjunction of the three. Answer: This is stated according to the analysis of the essence of seeing;
it does not refer to the case where they share the same essence as the basis.
If that were also being discussed, [it would be as follows].
Furthermore, they arise through the combination of three, four, and five [conditions] respectively,
because the mind and mental factors each have their own specific bases.
This explains their direct and manifest bases (*sākṣāt-pratyaya*).
It does not speak of remote [conditions] or seeds.
If it were to speak of remote supports and seeds, then dharmas would be manifold.
Question: If all mental factors arise based on contact, [how is this so]?
Why is it that the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in its third and fifty-fifth sections,
states that [the function of contact] is to serve as the basis for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*),
yet does not mention the remaining mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*)?
The treatise states:
"In the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it is said that by mentioning [the factor of] 'exertion' (*pragraha*), the others are included.
The commentary says:
Because this entity of volition (*cetanā*) is primary and preeminent: first, volition is the master of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
Thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* initially asks, "What is the aggregate of formations?

and replies, "It is the six groups of volition (*ṣaṭ-cetanākāyāḥ*). It then explains its own [definition] by stating, "Because it is the leader. Second, volition is preeminent in its ability to produce various karmas.
The mention of "volition" (cetanā) implies the inclusion of all other mental factors;
it does not refer to volition alone.
Therefore, all mental concomitants arise in dependence upon contact (sparśa).

Question: If that is so, why do the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and the first chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* state that the function of the [feeling] aggregate and so forth is "to serve as a basis for sensation"? Answer:
[The text continues...]
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other treatises state that [feeling] is superior because it reaches nearness.
The commentary says:
This is a general summary of the reasons why there is only feeling.
What constitutes the proximate [attainment], and is it also superior?
Treatise:
This means that because the objects grasped by contact (sparśa) are conducive to the production of excellence.
[The commentary] states:
The objects grasped by contact are the agreeable, the disagreeable, and those that are neutral between the two.
It is extremely proximate to the characteristics of being agreeable, disagreeable, or neutral toward that which is grasped as an object of perception.
"Extreme proximity" means similarity; it refers to such characteristics as being pleasant to the mind and so forth.
Because their characteristics, such as being concordant and beneficial,
are extremely similar in their modes of activity (*ākāra*),
they are called "adjacent" (*sāmantaka*).
As there is a common worldly expression that "this object" and "that object" are extremely similar—
wherein they are similar and adjacent in substance, possessing the same essence but different names—
this interpretation refers to the proximity of their objects. Furthermore, contact (sparśa) induces feeling (vedanā) more powerfully than other mental factors.
Therefore, when contact contacts suffering and so forth,
feeling experiences suffering and so forth;
in the states of the three feelings, contact and feeling are identical.
This understanding is called "superior" because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is similar [to that of the object];
others do not apprehend such agreeable characteristics or states such as suffering.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other treatises do not state that [contact] is the basis [of feeling]. Question:

Since contact resembles the triad of conditions and is termed "discriminative transformation," does feeling, which resembles contact, also take the name "discriminative contact"? Answer: To resolve this difficulty, it should be understood upon reaching the section on feeling.
However, in the present Mahāyāna,
it is held that the substance of contact (*sparśa*) is real, just as in the Sarvāstivāda;
this differs only from the view of a single master of the Sautrāntika school, for whom contact is produced by the conjunction of the three.
An opponent challenges the Mahāyāna, saying:
"If you say that contact is the conjunction of these three,
how can it possess a substantial entity?"
In order to refute that position, the treatise next states:
"However, the intrinsic nature of contact is real, not provisional."
The commentary states:
This establishes the thesis (*pakṣa*). The treatise (*śāstra*) [proceeds as follows].
"Because among the six groups of six dharmas, they are of the nature of mental factors (*caitasika*).
The commentary states:
"The following three reasons [are as follows]."
This is the first [point].
The *Abhidharmakośa* (Chapter 10), the *Nyāyānusāra*, and other texts state:
"It refers to the six internal bases (*ṣaḍ-ādhyātmikāyatana*)."
The six external bases, the six groups of consciousness, the six groups of craving, the six groups of contact, and the six groups of feeling.
Here, we take the "Six Sixes" from the *Dhātukāya-pāda-śāstra*, namely:

the six consciousnesses, the six contacts, the six feelings, the six perceptions, the six volitions, and the six cravings. The Sautrāntika school maintains that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is also substantially existent.
Because it is a state of volition (*cetanā*), it is not the same as a nominal contact (*prajñapti-sparśa*). The proof for refuting [that objection] is as follows:
Contact has a distinct substantial entity (*dravya*), because among the six groups of six dharmas, it is of the nature of a mental factor (*caitta*).
Regarding [the factors] such as sensation (*vedanā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), if one follows the sixfold and sixfold sets of phenomena in the *Abhidharmakośa*,
they are reckoned as being merely faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) and thus not substantially real. Therefore,
the term "mental factors" (*caitta*) is used to distinguish them from the aforementioned two [categories].
As extensively refuted in the tenth fascicle of the *Nyāyānusāra*,
the Śrāvakayāna treatise [argues] that [the intermediate state] is of the nature of nutriment.
The commentary states:
This second reason is that this enumeration of contact must necessarily be substantially existent,
because it possesses the nature of the four nutriments (*āhāra*).
Just as with the other three nutriments, since it is admitted that the odors, tastes, and tangibles of edible food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra) are real,
they are used as the analogy;
for the tangible elements (mahābhūta-spraṣṭavya) are indeed real.
This does not contradict the principle;
alternatively, one might argue that mental factors (*caitta*) should also extend to the lower realms,
as such a concise formulation would suffice.
Treatise:
Because it can serve as a condition.
Commentary says:
This is the third reason: furthermore, this enumeration of contact is definitely substantially existent,
because it is comprised among the mental factors within the members of dependent origination,
just as craving conditions grasping.
Because they exist as states of mental application (*manasikāra*), those [factors] are also admitted to be real;
all the members that are mental concomitants (*caitasika*) are substantially existent.
This is according to the system of other schools.
Even if only a small portion of the twelve links were substantially real, it could still serve as an analogy;
however, [the opponent] does not admit that even a small portion of contact is substantially real.
If a small portion is admitted to be substantially real, the remaining portions cannot be considered merely nominal.
Because there is no distinct cause.
The treatise states:
For example, the nature of sensation and so forth is not identical to the triad of conjunction.
The commentary states:
Regarding the phrase "feeling and so forth," the term "and so forth" (ādi) serves as an illustration for the two causes.
Furthermore, regarding the mental factors such as sensation (*vedanā*) mentioned in the first simile,
sensation may apply to both the first and second similes,
while the others apply only to the middle simile.
He refutes that Sautrāntika school by means of three reasons:
[the claim] that it is not the mere conjunction of the three is also stated as a second thesis-property (*pakṣadharma*).
There is no contradiction in this being a thesis-property. Within this, the Mahāyāna...
Contact has a distinct substantial entity and is not identical to the conjunction of the three. One master of the Sautrāntika school says that contact is constituted by the conjunction of the three;

thus, contact is that very conjunction and is conventional rather than real. Another master says that contact arises from the conjunction of the three, but contact is not itself the conjunction of the three. According to the Sarvāstivāda, although contact exists as a distinct entity, [it is not the same as the conjunction].
It cannot differentiate and produce minds, mental factors (*citta-caitta*), and so forth through transformation;
its function is solely to serve as the basis for feeling (*vedanā*) and the other [mental factors]. Thus, the three categories are distinct.
[End of] Treatise.
"Mental attention (manasikāra) has the function of directing and drawing the mind.
Commentary: This explains the second number.
The text is intelligible. First, the essence and activity are briefly clarified;
next, they are explained extensively;
finally, they are refuted.
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and other texts state: "What is meant by 'arousing the mind' (*cittasaṃvejana*)? How does one arouse the mind? In what stage does one arouse the mind? [The answer is:
"Once it has already arisen, how could there be any further need for arousal?"
Since that which has already arisen has already passed, it cannot alert what has not yet arisen;
thus, all minds ought to be alerted.
However, the attention capable of providing such an alert has likewise not yet arisen.
How can it be alerted?
The treatise states:
This alerting reaches its culmination; therefore, it is called attention (*manasikāra*).
The commentary states:
This refers to the stage when attention and the other factors have not yet arisen;
at that time, the seed of attention [remains].
The "object-awakening" (viṣayābhisaṃskāra) refers to the seeds of the mind that are capable of arising toward a specific object;

it does not refer to awakening all seeds of the mind, for those have not yet encountered their conditions and thus do not necessarily arise. There are two functional powers of attention (manasikāra) in awakening the mind.
First, it causes the mind that has not yet arisen to arise;
second, it causes the mind that has already arisen to move toward its object.
Thus it is said that it awakens the seeds of the mind that ought to arise, inducing them to proceed toward their objects.
The masters of the Nyāya school state that the function of attention (manasikāra) arises in the future;
this is likewise true for the meaning and force of seeds (bīja).

It should be understood that, like other minds, it is not the primary cause of maturation (*vipāka*);
this indicates that its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is difficult to discern and differs from that of other consciousnesses.
If one were to allow for easy detachment [from seeds], then neither the wholesome nor the unwholesome realms of existence would be able to mutually contain their respective seeds.

the third fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* also offers this interpretation: "If there is an interruption..."
It would then not be born from that [cause],

This consciousness is extremely indistinct;

Because the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of wisdom and mindfulness are extremely distinct, [this consciousness] is unable to differentiate between the characteristics of disagreeable and agreeable objects.
This demonstrates that it is exclusively associated with the feeling of equanimity (upekṣā-vedanā), and not with suffering or pleasure;
furthermore, it distinguishes it from being concurrent with the wholesome or the defiled, as well as from subtle conditions,
and distinguishes it from meditative absorption (samāpatti) and non-resultant (avipāka) states.
Because the characteristics of non-vipāka dharmas are coarse and mobile,
meditative absorption (*samādhi*) deeply grasps its object;
these [non-vipāka dharmas], being spontaneous and subtle, do not grasp it deeply— this is the meaning of "a single category."
To briefly explain the number of resolute understandings (*adhimokṣa*):
because there is a resolute understanding at the time when one first fixes upon an object that was previously indeterminate, they proceed in a continuous succession.
This demonstrates the absence of desire.

By these five points, the second [section] correctly reveals the reason why only equanimity (*upekṣā*) is established.

As for the remaining four conditions, because they are distinguished by their objects and so forth, they are associated only with equanimity (*upekṣā*). Although there are two interpretations, the former is superior;

One should not exclude its specific objects and so forth therein.
The treatise further states: "Moreover, this association extends only to the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*)."

Treatise:
Regarding the four kinds of phenomena, to which category do they belong?
Commentary states:
This is the first question. There are four kinds of phenomena (*dharma*).
By what phenomena are they subsumed? The Mahāyāna also possesses intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), goodness (*kuśala*), and so forth, as explained in the original commentary.
These three natures may each be divided into two:
first, the conventional.
Second is the ultimate [perspective].
Conditioned wholesome dharmas are called mundane wholesomeness because they bring about desirable results, both worldly and supramundane.
Because they are coarse, subject to arising and ceasing, and lack security, [conditioned phenomena] are not ultimately wholesome.
Unconditioned wholesome dharmas are called "ultimately wholesome" because their nature is supreme tranquility and security. All extremely evil dharmas are called "conventionally unwholesome."
Because they can bring about coarse, manifest, and undesirable fruits,
all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena are called "ultimately unwholesome" (*paramārthākuśala*).
Because their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is heavy and unstable, conditioned neutral (*saṃskṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena are called "conventionally neutral" (*saṃvṛtyavyākṛta*).
They cannot produce results that are either pleasant or unpleasant;

because their intrinsic nature is coarse and heavy (*dausthulya*), they are confused with the unwholesome. Space and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are termed "ultimately indeterminate" (*paramārtha-avyākṛta*).
It does not attract two fruits, because there is no confusion [between them]. Alternatively, each may be divided into three.
Regarding the three types of wholesome [karma]: first, wholesome [karma] that produces desirable results.
That is to say, wholesome contaminated phenomena are "skillful wholesomeness" (*kauśalya-kuśala*).
Wholesome conditioned phenomena are "wholesomeness as security" (*kṣema-kuśala*). Unconditioned wholesome phenomena are "wholesomeness as peace" (*āśvāsa-kuśala*).
Regarding the three types of unwholesome [phenomena]: first, there is that which is unwholesome because it brings about undesirable results.
First, the unwholesome by way of being extremely evil, which refers to the two natures that lack skillful means;
second, the unwholesome by way of being afflicted, which refers to the three natures that lack peace and security;
and third, the unwholesome by way of being with outflows, which refers to all contaminated phenomena. Regarding the three types of the indeterminate: first, the indeterminate by way of association.

That is to say: first, the indeterminate mind and mental factors; second, the two types of dissociated indeterminate phenomena, namely indeterminate matter and dissociated formations; and third, the truly indeterminate.
That is to say, space and non-analytical cessation. Alternatively, each may be divided into four.
Regarding the four types of the wholesome: first, that which is wholesome by its own nature (*svabhāva-kuśala*).
That is to say: first, the eleven mental factors beginning with faith, which are exclusively wholesome;
second, associated wholesomeness, referring to the mind and mental factors associated with faith and the others; and third, co-arising wholesomeness.
This refers to all wholesome forms (*rūpa*) and dissociated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*).
By extension, the same applies to seeds that are wholesome. Fourth is ultimate wholesomeness (*paramārthakuśala*), which refers to wholesome unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
Regarding the four types of unwholesome [phenomena]: first is unwholesomeness by intrinsic nature (*svabhāvakuśala*).
That is to say: first, the ten unwholesome mental factors such as lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and so forth;
second, associated unwholesomeness, which refers to the mind and mental factors associated with those [unwholesome factors]; and third, derivative unwholesomeness.
That is to say: unwholesome form and dissociated formations;
the seeds are also like this. Fourth, unwholesome in the ultimate sense.
That is to say, there are tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*). Regarding the four types of neutral (*avyākṛta*) [phenomena]:
first, the neutral of transformation, which refers to all neutral minds and mental factors; second, the neutral of that which is transformed.
That is to say: first, neutral (avyākṛta) form-dharmas;
second, their seeds are likewise; third, neutral states of the three stages, namely neutral dissociated dharmas;
and fourth, neutral in the ultimate sense (paramārtha-avyākṛta).

That is to say, [it refers to] space and non-analytical cessation; as explained in the various gateways concerning the wholesome and so forth at the end of the third chapter and the beginning of the fourth volume of the Abhidharma, all of those are interpreted by means of this same principle.
In this regard, each point should be understood according to reason.

Wholesome [karma] has a desirable fruit,

This master’s intention is to explain that,
by analogy, the five aspects are identical in their essential nature as consciousness.

however, there are only four [remaining], excluding the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), all modes (*sarvākāra*), the aspect of activity (*ākāra*), and that which is associated with equanimity (*upekṣā-sahagata*).
The continuity of cause and effect is not severed;
the specific stages of transition and relinquishment will be explained later in the relevant section.
This example applies to what precedes it, as it should be understood accordingly. Question: The fundamental consciousness is accompanied by five factors;
are contact and the others likewise?
Although contact does not correspond with itself,
these five factors are analogous in their mode of association.
The aspect of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is precisely that of discernment (*vijñapti*).
Contact (sparśa) functions according to its appropriate mode of activity,
causing the mind and mental factors to come into contact with the preceding object;

"The same difficulty applies to other examples. Response: "Because the other categories are mutually inclusive, they may all be cited as analogies.

it would also cause contact and the others to all become identical [to it].
If [feeling] associated with equanimity were not included within feeling,
then the same fault would logically apply to feeling and the other [aggregates].

because contact and so forth are not subject to any distinction [in their arising], they extend all the way down to the level of non-discrimination.

however, because they lack autonomy, they are not themselves capable of perfuming. Answer: Mental factors possess the quality of increase and decrease, and thus they are fully capable of being perfumed.

Conditioned by the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and the five [sensory] groups, there are six types of perfumable [objects]; thus, there are six instances of perfuming.

it was not meant to say that entering into quiescence constitutes a "common" answer.
Regarding the abandonment [of the seeds] within the *ālayavijñāna*, this has already been explained and need not be repeated here.
Treatise:
Since mind and its associates are common [to all], they should be explained according to their respective meanings.
Commentary: [As follows].
This means that these minds and so forth follow along with defiled attachment and concealment;
regardless of which vehicle [one follows],
they are only abandoned at the stage of the vajra-mind or from the eighth bhūmi onwards.
If one who is in the state of maturation (*vipāka*) also abandons the mind, then it is abandoned at the time when those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) enter *nirvāṇa*.
However, for one whose mind is untainted (*anāsrava*), there is no time of abandonment. Regarding the phrase "the mind and so forth":
That is to say, the support of the knowable,
the appropriating consciousness (*ādānavijñāna*), and so forth; or, regarding the meaning of "mind" (*citta*),
it refers to the stage of the bodhisattva while still on the path.
The two vehicles' state of no-more-learning possesses actual perfuming;
the Buddha has no perfuming;
the former [the two vehicles] possess prior perfuming.
The Tathāgata also possesses seeds of perfuming;
these may likewise be termed "mind.
Treatise.
"However, regarding the eighth consciousness reaching the objects of appropriation," the commentary states:
"The preceding eight sections and ten points have completed the explanation of the root verses."
The following is the second section, which provides a general summary and analysis.
Regarding the causes and effects of this consciousness as discussed within the Three Vehicles,
there are, in total, two stages.
First, the stage with outflows (*sāsrava*),
which comprises all stages prior to those of the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages and the two vehicles (*yāna*) who have attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
It is exclusively of an indeterminate nature and is comprised within the category of karmic maturation (*vipāka*).
Although those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and others have already severed all such karma, [it remains].
Because it is summoned by prior karma, the force of that past karma is also termed "maturation" (vipāka). It is associated only with the five mental factors, such as contact (*sparśa*) and so forth;
it takes as its objects only what was previously described: the appropriated body of the sense faculties, seeds, and the spheres of objects. Here, "sphere" (*āyatana*) refers to the locus.
This consists of three gates:
namely, nature (svabhāva), concomitance (sahabhū), and object (ālambana).
These differ from those in the preceding ten gates regarding the Buddha.
Regarding the analysis herein, those that are identical need not be discussed;
namely, the three gateways of self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), resultant characteristic (*phalalakṣaṇa*), and relinquishment (*tyāga*), were already explained immediately prior.
Some say this refers to the stage of being with outflows (*sāsrava*).
This reveals the previous two and the subsequent one among the gates.
Its causal characteristic—the aspect of all-seeds—is unknowable and discernible; it functions perpetually in association with equanimity, as it pervades both cause and fruit.
This was not explained therein; however,
because the causes and effects differ according to their nature (*svabhāva*), their association (*sahabhū*),
and their object (*ālambana*), they are now analyzed.
However, because there is a concern that [the term] "associated with feeling" might be overextended to the stage of a cause,
the untainted (anāsrava) stage is specifically cited to exclude it.
This is done to demonstrate that this particular class remains unchanged.
Treatise:
The two untainted stages are comprised solely within the nature of the wholesome (*kuśala*).
Commentary states:
This belongs solely to the stage of the Tathāgata;
it does not belong to Bodhisattvas or those of the Two Vehicles,
as their fruition is not yet complete.
Because its merit is inferior and because the four wisdoms have not yet been attained,
this untainted state is exclusively of a wholesome nature.
Because the Tathāgata possesses no dharma of karmic maturation;
because his body is not summoned by karma or afflictions;
and because all his merits are perfectly fulfilled.
There is nothing that is not unwholesome.
Treatise:
[This refers to] the twenty-one [factors], up to each of the five wholesome [factors] and the eleven.
The commentary states:
When both the provisional and the real are considered together, there are twenty-one [mental factors].
This is because non-negligence (*apramāda*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) exist as provisional entities.
If discussed according to their actual nature, there are only eighteen:
non-negligence and equanimity are both comprised within the three wholesome roots; diligence is a portion of them;
and non-harming is a portion of the wholesome root of non-hatred.
This refers to the five universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*) and the five object-specific factors (*viniyata*),
which together with the eleven wholesome factors (*kuśala*) total twenty-one.
Why, then, are they associated with the universal mental factors?
Treatise:
Because it is always associated with all minds. Commentary:
[As stated above.]
Since the five dharmas, such as contact (*sparśa*), are always associated with all minds,
they exist even in the untainted (*anāsrava*) state.
Why, then, are there distinct mental objects (*viṣaya-viśeṣa*)?
Treatise:
Because one constantly and joyfully seeks to realize and know the object of observation.
Commentary states:
From this, desire arises;
because desire does not diminish,
it takes the aspect of a desirable object.
Treatise:
Because it constantly maintains its seal upon the object under observation. Commentary:
[As stated above.]
Therefore, there is resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
One maintains this through resolute conviction;
thus, the Buddha has no doubt regarding the object.
Because there is constant mental retention,
resolute conviction does not diminish.
Treatise:
"Because one constantly maintains clear mindfulness regarding objects previously experienced.
The commentary states:
"From this, there arises mindfulness (smṛti)."
This means that because there is clear recollection regarding objects previously experienced,
mindfulness does not diminish.
Treatise:
Because the World-Honored One possesses no unsettled mind.
Commentary states:
Therefore, they possess meditative concentration;
because they constantly enter concentration at all times,
they have no distracted mind.
Concentration never diminishes;
for it is the constant discernment of all phenomena.
The commentary states: Therefore, it is said that there is wisdom;
it is not the case that one speaks out of ignorance regarding the objects of cognition.
Nor is it erroneous cognition;
because it is constant discernment, wisdom (prajñā) certainly exists,
and that wisdom never diminishes.
Therefore, the five object-specific mental factors can also be associated [with one another].
If one is in the causal stage, a single mind at a single time does not take the past or future as its objects;
the Tathāgata is not like this.
Therefore, although that Tathāgata gives rise to mindfulness and desire to recall with longing all objective signs from the past and future,
he always takes as his object those phenomena of the present and so forth.
Because one realizes and understands each [object] individually,
mindfulness and desire coexist.
Why are there eleven [factors], such as the wholesome and so forth?
Treatise:
Because it is constantly associated with supreme pure faith and so forth. Commentary:
[As stated above].
These eleven wholesome factors are present by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*) in all concentrated minds;
this is because the Tathāgata has attained the four types of verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*).
It must be associated with faith and so forth.
According to the treatise, this is because it is undefiled.
The commentary states:
The six fundamental afflictions, such as greed, along with the twenty-two secondary afflictions, are by nature defiled;
therefore, they necessarily do not coexist.
Question: For what reason is it not associated with the indeterminate?
Treatise:
Because there is no distraction.
The commentary states:
In the meditative mind, remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) are necessarily absent;
they exist only in the distracted mind. Furthermore, among the two types—vitarka and vicāra—it is primarily these that give rise to the gates of body and speech.
These [vitarka and vicāra] are subsumed under coarse movement.
The body and speech of the Tathāgata manifest spontaneously and are perpetually serene;
therefore, he is without vitarka and vicāra. Do these vitarka and vicāra also pertain to the untainted (anāsrava) states and so forth?
This shall be explained in the section on the "Lower Indefinites" (*aniyata*) below.

However, it is not said that the Buddha also possesses vitarka and vicāra. Question: Is heedfulness (*apramāda*) a dependent designation (*upādāya-prajñapti*), while the wisdom of the Tathāgata is said to be associated [with it]?
Vitarka and vicāra depend upon either volition (cetanā) or wisdom (prajñā).
The Tathāgata should also possess them. Answer: Because non-negligence (apramāda) and so forth cease evil causes and effects, they are present in both states.
Investigation (*vitarka*) and analysis (*vicāra*) exist only in the stage of the cause;

therefore, the Tathāgata said they do not exist [in the fruit]. Question: Since the Buddha has already eliminated all evil and possesses non-negligence (*apramāda*), the Buddha, though perfected in the fruit, should still possess investigation and analysis. Answer: These [two] initiate bodily and vocal actions.
Furthermore, it is not spontaneous;
since the Buddha has already perfected the fruit,
he has no need for it.
Evil must be deeply guarded against.
Although one’s merit may be full, one must remain free from negligence and the like. Question: Does the Buddha not indeed manifest bodily and verbal actions?
There is no logical impediment to allowing that it may be untainted (*anāsrava*);
why, then, is this not accepted? If it were not so, it would contradict the explanations in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* and other texts, as one shall know from below.
Treatise:
This also functions only in equality with the ultimate. Commentary:
[As stated above.]
Furthermore, just as the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) in its causal state corresponds only to the sensation of equanimity (upekṣā-vedanā),
because it always functions spontaneously and effortlessly.
Because it does not engage in conceptual discrimination;
because it is not something that can be easily discarded;
and because it is immovable.

As stated in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, this wisdom is immovable and unlike other forms of knowledge. Upon which meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) does this wisdom arise? Some say it pervades the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) and the six stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Because one traverses and contemplates the untainted supernormal powers (*anāsrava-abhijñā*) in this stage,
those that arise as manifest activity belong only to the fourth dhyāna,
as they primarily rely upon the celestial abodes (*devasthāna*).
This wisdom arises for the most part from great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*),
which exists only in the fourth dhyāna;
this serves as the root of virtue.
Because merit primarily relies upon the fourth dhyāna,

as stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (Treatise on the Collection) chapter seven and the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* (Commentary on the Collection) chapter fourteen. Some say it extends through the six lower dhyānas,
as there is no logical reason to exclude them.
The realm of form possesses minds that take everything as their object,
whereas the formless realm does not; even if the formless were to possess such [minds], [it would be different].
Because it cannot universally take all things as its object in every moment of thought,
it exists only within the six stages of the form realm;
however, those who constantly dwell in that fourth dhyāna [possess it].
Because it is preeminent,
although it exists in the lower stages,
it remains exclusively an equanimous feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
Because the feeling of equanimity (upekṣā-vedanā) is tranquil and unshakable,
and because it is immutable,
the *Ālaya-vijñāna* is said in the sixty-third [treatise] to be accompanied by the feeling of equanimity.
In the state of the three feelings, they proceed together without interruption.
It should be understood that the remaining three feelings are induced by reflection (*manasikāra*) and are not innate (*sahaja*);
they manifest before one at various times through the application of attention.
Because those co-nascent feelings are extremely subtle, they are difficult to distinguish.
These three feelings are namely suffering, pleasure, and equanimity;
that is to say, the "other" refers to the neutral [feeling].

In this stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*), because the causal condition (*anvayakāraṇa*) is the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), the two feelings of pleasure (*sukha*) and joy (*prīti*) cannot arise;
for these are induced by mental reflection (*manasikāra*). Some say that [this state] exists only in the fourth dhyāna.
In the other stages, these are entirely absent. It is taught in sixty-nine [treatises] that the Tathāgata’s qualities mostly rely upon the fourth [dhyāna].
This is to be understood by analogy with entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Among these three explanations, the first interpretation is superior.
Although this wisdom exists in both the form and formless realms, when one cultivates its seeds there,
it necessarily does not manifest,
just as the conventional wisdom (saṃvṛtijñāna) associated with the three types of limit-attainment (samāpatti) does not manifest.
Because it is not easily abandoned and because it is unshakable,
even if one attains the untainted stages (anāsrava-bhūmi) throughout the ten stages (daśa-bhūmi).
This poses no obstacle to reason;
it is merely a matter of contemplative observation,
and thus does not contradict principle.
This concludes the second section, the analysis of the gate of correspondence.
The treatise states: "Because all dharmas reach all dharmas."
The commentary states:
This explains the objects of perception.
It takes as its objects the eighteen realms, both conditioned and unconditioned.
Because mirror-like wisdom universally takes all phenomena as its object,
it is able to take the self-nature of mind and its associates, as well as their associated mental factors, as objects;
furthermore, its seeing portion also manifests the image of its own self-verifying portion.
Together with their associated mental factors and reflections,
it is therefore called "omniscience" (*sarvajñatā*),
as has already been explained in the second fascicle.
*Buddhabhūmi*, Chapter Four, Part Two, Scroll Ten: Analysis of Various Gates. Part Two, Section Seven:

Explaining which consciousnesses of which realms transform to produce the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) and the others. Thus concludes the preceding general analysis of the eighth consciousness through ten gates.
This follows the structure of the verses.
If one takes the fundamental consciousness as the primary example for associated dharmas,
there are eleven gates.
If explained individually and in detail,
there would be an infinite number of points;
each one should be explained according to the specific categories as previously set forth.
The first of the various gateways for the analytical explanation of the verses is hereby concluded.
*Commentary on the Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, Scroll Three, End.
